Jacob opened his eyes and reached for the dagger at his belt. He stopped breathing, his eyes widening as he absorbed the advancing darkness. Then, from the encroaching fog — a tendril shot toward Jonas — curling around his ankle like a deadly snake. Suddenly, the boy released a blood-curdling scream, and Jacob lunged forward, but—

It was too late!

And Jonas was instantly yanked away and dragged into the deadly fog as his terrified cries faded into the murk. Cautiously, Jacob went after him, pushing forward into the darkness. It wasn't long before he came upon a monstrous Almond Tree he half-remembered from a fairy tale. It had rotting human limbs as branches, and on those branches dangled thirty-four heads caught in agonizing screams.

Jacob continued through the fog after the boy, swinging his dagger in wild arcs, slicing through the vicious tendrils that reached for him, his movements growing increasingly desperate with each passing second.

"Boy! Where are you? Speak!"

As if in answer a tendril wrapped around Jacob's wrist. Instantly, he yanked his arm away with a scream. Then he heard something—

Something familiar.

A voice.

It came again and again.

"Jacob... Help me, brother!"

Jacob froze. "Wilhelm?" He peered into the darkness. "Wilhelm!"
27C894FD4B18A3FC1B75B18B0F3AEE62:
"Wilhelm!" Jacob yelled. "Where are you?"

No answer came. Only the sound of his ragged breathing and the inhuman howls of creatures moving through the fog came to him. Each creature appeared more menacing than the last as if the fog were inspired by his memories, pulling from a palette of horrors from his fairy tale collection.

"Brother, where are you..." Jacob muttered, evading a tendril. "Is this what I get for playing hero?" He remembered their childhood games and how he'd always play the role of hero in whatever imaginary story they had concocted. There had been so many games. So many stories. He sighed and hoped Wilhem was okay wherever he was.

As he thought about Wilhelm, tendrils of fog suddenly wrapped around his legs. With a start, he contorted his body and swung his dagger in wild, chaotic arcs, making the tendrils disappear. Still, his movements became increasingly desperate as the tendrils continued to manifest and slither up his body, crushing his chest and lungs.

Was this how it ended?

Suffocated by fog. Attacked by the shadowy creatures from the tales he and his brother had spent their lives collecting? No. His story couldn't end like this. Their story couldn't end like this!

With this thought, he summoned every ounce of strength left within, and with a terrible roar, he twisted and broke free from the fog's stranglehold. Instantly, he stumbled backward, gasping for air, the fog suddenly dissipating before his very eyes.

Within moments, the village stood silent, bathed in dying sunlight. There was no sign of the horrors that had assailed him just moments before. Somewhere, his horse nickered to let Jacob know he was okay.

Jacob took a calming breath and ran a shaky hand through his sweat-soaked hair. He looked down at his dagger in his white-knuckled grip. No blood, no gore, nothing. Just clean steel. He didn't understand any of it.

Then he felt the presence of things unseen observing him, measuring him, relishing his suffering. He had no idea how to explain it, nor did he think it could be explained. But what he felt was... toyed with. Like the fog were a giant black cat playing with a wounded mouse.

I'm losing my mind, he thought to himself. The fog isn't alive. It isn't watching me. I've heard too many stories, and my imagination is getting the better of me. This carnage has nothing to do with fog. Perhaps an attack from a neighboring village. Perhaps revenge. Perhaps a feud. Perhaps... something else...

Jacob didn't want to think about it as he made his way to his horse, his boots scuffing the dirt. Fear and frustration knotted inside him. He was exhausted and more scared than he had ever been in his life, yet he refused to return home without his brother.

And so, Jacob pushed the fear out of his mind and remembered the good nights—the nights when his father would keep them up wide-eyed with wonder with stories by the crackling fire. The stories had captivated and inspired them, so much so that they would spend the rest of their lives chasing stories and sharing them with the rest of the world.

Reaching his horse, Jacob grabbed the reins and swung himself into the saddle. Then, scanning the village one last time, he muttered a silent prayer for the boy, and nudged his horse forward just as—

A songbird landed on his horse's nose.

The bird glanced at him for a long moment before taking flight, guiding him toward the outskirts of the village, where the road ahead vanished into a dense, shadowy tree line.

Hold on, Wilhelm, he thought. I'm coming for you, brother.

And as he passed beneath the first trees, darkness enveloped them so that Jacob's hand instinctively tightened on his dagger, ready for whatever horrors might wait in the depths of this dark, twisted fairy tale.
268E19E74A775E1DC17A238ADF97A008:
The sound of Archie’s hands pounding against the door feels a hundred miles away. Evan ascends the staircase. Each step feels lighter than the last. He just needs a little break. No fake friends. No overbearing boss. No unions, no maggots, no lies, no mine.

No killing.

He figures if he calls the fire department to let his father out, it would take them a few minutes to get here. By then, he could be long gone. Find a new place to call home. Maybe down the coast. Somewhere a little sunnier.

As he reaches the top of the stairs he notices something pooling around his feet. Smoke? He turns around and barrels back down the stairs.

The smoke feels like soup as he descends, pitch-black and choking. Too thick for smoke… fog? He can’t hear his father screaming anymore. As it chokes out the light, it also seems to choke out sound.

Evan calls to his father, but the fog swallows his voice. He lurches forward, arms outstretched. Each step feels like it should be the last, but the staircase keeps descending. Finally, after what feels like a lifetime, his foot hits solid ground.

He places his hands on the wall, feeling his way around to the door, but these walls aren’t right. Cold. Rough. Slick to the touch. The fog begins to dissipate, just enough to see his own hands.

Blood.

He gasps as the room comes into view. The steel door is gone, the grey concrete walls replaced by rickety wooden boards. Streaks of gore reach from floor to ceiling as exposed pipes rattle erratically.

His eyes scan for anything familiar. Where his father might be trapped. As he reaches the center of the room, his gaze freezes. An enormous structure, covered in meat hooks. He is unable to tear his eyes away from it. The structure horrifies him, but something strange and foreign speaks deep within him:

These hooks… these are my hooks.
92E870724F07D4DE3AA5B9A4DBA21E23:
The feeling in the pit of his stomach is too much for him. He turns and stumbles back up the stairs. The ascent feels endless. Every muscle in his body aches, his lungs burn, but he pushes upward. Out of this basement. Out of this nightmare.

At the top, he finds himself... nowhere. No mine. No estate. Nothing but unending, rocky ground in every direction, and that damned fog again.

He picks a direction and starts walking. He remembers being young, hunting with his father, getting separated, lost in the woods. Back then, he walked straight until he hit a road, got his bearings, got back to the car. Got an earful from his father. His fists tighten. He supposes he'll get another earful when he finds him... if he finds him.

The thought makes his stomach drop. How long has he been walking? He cannot remember. It feels like it's been days. He can barely remember the basement where he left his father... as if he hadn't seen it in years. A smeared, grey memory. But that other basement... it sits heavy, vivid in his mind. As if he never left. He can still count the planks on the wall. And those hooks. He could almost... hear them. Calling out to him.

He snaps out of his reverie as a sharp, crushing pain shoots up his leg. He collapses, shrieks in pain. Looks down.

His father's bear trap.

He shouts out again, frustrated. Who did this? The same person who brought him here, who separated him from his father? He pries it open, wrests his ankle from its grip. Blood gushes from the jagged wound. He looks around again, desperate for some sign of humanity... nothing. I'll die here, he thinks. I just wanted to get away. He drops to his seat, wraps his arm around the trap, and passes out as the fog muffles his pained screams.
F9710FE14CA12BB30E67FBA5103DCF03:
Evan comes to, gasps. Grabs at his leg. Dry. He exhales. No wound. It throbs with pain, but the skin is smooth, undamaged. Evan wonders if he imagined the entire thing.

His eyes adapt to the darkness and his surroundings come into view... not imagined. He is back in that basement. With that structure. Again.

He shouts in frustration, what do you want from me? His words bounce hollowly off the ramshackle walls. Nobody is here to answer. He props his hand against the wall, shakily rises to his feet, heads to the staircase again.

As he limps towards it, each step becomes harder--not due to the pain, but as if some kind of magnet is pulling him back. As if something is telling him, you are not meant to leave. Stop resisting.

He pushes forward regardless. He's no sheep... no maggot. Whatever game this place is playing with him, he will not participate. He looks down at the first step, gingerly places his aching foot on it, pushes onward.

This time, the pain is in his shoulder.

He did not notice the chains hanging from the ceiling… nor the fetid, rusting hooks dangling from them.

He does not scream this time. It feels pointless. Nobody is listening… or if they are, his screams mean nothing. He grabs onto the hook, tries to pry it from his arm, but it is stuck fast. He instead tears it from the chain. Takes another shaky step.

Another hook tucks into his torso, just under his rib cage. He groans and tears it from its chain. Looks up the stairs. Chains, all the way up. Dangling at impossible angles. A grim metallic web.

He grits his teeth, pushes on. He thinks back to when his father used to lock him in that very room. That feeling of helplessness, of being trapped. He ducks, dodges, moves the hooks aside with his hands, but hooks barb him with every step. And with every step he tears another from its chain. The stairs have no light at the top of them. No hope. He does not know why he keeps pressing forward. Only that he will not be trapped again.

He reaches the top of the stairs, bleeding and losing consciousness again, he cannot help but laugh. Because of course.

That damned basement again.
5AEC5AF94F6CF9106AA49FB8B9D38691:
He has not left the basement for a long, long time.

There is no food, but he does not starve; just feels a vague hollowness. The stairs are pointless. He has slammed the walls, shouted, tried to sleep, but nothing changes. The blood continues to pour down the walls. The pipes continue to rattle. And the structure continues to reach out to him.

He decides to focus on it. He's tried everything else. He picks up his bear trap, the one familiar thing in this realm, and ambles over to the structure, places a hand on it. Closes his eyes.

What he sees is a memory. Not his own memory... someone else's. A moonlit forest. Weak, anguished cries in the distance. The point of view shuffles forward, towards it. A man. Lying, on the ground, in a bear trap.

Evan's uncle.

Archie... get me out...

He feels his father's voice as if it resonates from his own throat. Roland... what have you gotten yourself into?

Roland whimpers, tugs feebly at the trap, cries out again. Brother... please!

Evan feels the creases of his father's face sharpen as he frowns. Weak. Pathetic, wretched, weak, idiot, maggot! His right hand grips the blade of a meat cleaver. Can't even hunt bear right! Raises the cleaver…

Evan gasps as he returns to his own body. It felt so… real. The evening frost in his lungs, the dimples of the cleaver's handle. The hate.

He looks at the structure again, with a new understanding. This place didn't take me from him. It saved me from him. His violence. His control.

He gently wraps his fingers around one of the structure's hooks. Pulls it, tests its resistance. He acutely feels that hollowness again—a hunger, a longing. He asks again, earnestly this time... what do you want from me?

As if in response, an animalistic growl erupts from the staircase.
A90183464368D88EA7959488A613B564:
Evan whips around, faces the stairs. A lumbering frame approaches him, slowly. A twisted, makeshift cleaver in its hand. Matted brown fur sticks to its face, its snout gleams red with blood in the basement light. It gnashes its teeth, snarls, speaks.

Maggot.

Evan does not cower as he once might have. His father would always make him feel so small, so alone. But here, Evan is not alone. He calmly sets the bear trap. Dares the beast to come at him.

It sees the trap, hesitates. Where did you find that?

Saw it in the forest, Evan responds. Saw what you did.

The beast roars, charges at Evan. Evan shifts his weight, kicks the trap into the beast's path. A sickening crunch bounces off the basement walls, and the beast crumples.

No! It snarls, growls, snaps its jaw at Evan. Drops the cleaver to pry his leg from the trap. Without thought, Evan snatches the cleaver from the ground. Feels that rush of blood, just as his father had. Raises his arm. Pauses.

No... not a kill.

A sacrifice.

He grabs the beast by its shoulders, lifts it, and slams its back onto a hook. It screams out in shock. Throws its arms to its back, tries to unhook itself, but its body is too massive, its arms too short. It flails and screams as Evan walks back to the wall, holds the cleaver in his hand, feels its weight. He watches silently as the fight leaves the beast. The hollowness in Evan’s chest dissolves, replaced by a new feeling… fulfillment.

He basks in this feeling for a long time. Impossible to tell how long. He watches the beast give up. Watches its skin dry, peel, explode with maggots. Watches the desiccated meat flop to the floor. Watches the maggots consume the flesh, leaving behind only bones.

He picks up the beast's femur, begins to carve into the bone with his cleaver. Whittles a face, a jaw. Affixes the beast's teeth. A smile... something beautiful from something so ugly. Pulls the crude sculpture over his face. A symbol of his devotion to this basement, that saved him from his father. Saved him from himself.

He hears voices again, this time distant, up the stairs. He grabs the trap, his cleaver, ascends the stairs. Nothing stops him this time. He feels weightless as he ascends, as he once had so long ago. At the top, flickering light and crackling embers dance and sing in the distance, a group huddled around its warmth.

Evan looks at them from a distance for a long time. Thinks of the basement. How it accepted him. Molded him. Delivered him.

Perhaps it will deliver them too.
1D58372B4408DE8487E2F996F8600AD4:
Sunlight spills over Renjiro Yamaoka sitting cross-legged in the meadow. His horse, Rai-Fu, waits patiently. The samurai inhales, considers the weight of the katana at his hip.

His mind wanders for a second, the calm disrupted. His chest tightens. The green fields before him offer no peace when he knows his son spills the red blood of innocents upon them.

He is on the trail to stop him: Kazan, the man known as the Oni, his son who has made it his mission to purify the samurai—not through discipline or honor but by massacring the farmers who oppose them. A savage reaction to minor transgressions.

The sun carves its way through the sky as Rai-Fu carries Renjiro along a quiet road. Modest homes dot the field ahead. No one toils outside. There is an unlikely stillness, as if he journeys through a painting. In the distance, a man watches, leaning against his home. He does not move.

As Renjiro approaches, the scene becomes clear. The farmer is impaled on the wall of his home. Blood pools at his feet. A crow takes flight. It ignores the corpse, instead landing further down the hill. Renjiro follows. A pool of pitch-blackness shuffles in the tall grass ahead. The dark stain screeches, a vast murder of crows lambasting the intruder. Reluctantly, they take flight, stretching across the sky like a dark scythe. Bloods soaks the earth where they stood. There are hints that the viscera is human—a roughly cut hand, an exposed femur—but the number of victims is impossible to know in the pulverized gore.

This cannot be the work of Kazan. How could he—

A sour lump rises in Renjiro’s throat. He wonders if the commoners’ tales are true.

It must be an oni that possesses Kazan for his son could never commit such evil.
7C578EC7402E6EA5704289B62FFB9A94:
Renjiro’s slumps with fatigue. He hears the voice in his head.

Go home. You are no samurai.

He is tired. He acknowledges the truth:

I am no samurai.

The voice demands more.

You are not Renjiro Yamaoka.

He nods.

I am not Renjiro Yamaoka.

The faded memories return. He is a child, torn from his parents. He does not understand why. They scream his name…

Hachi!

He never sees them again. He’s brought to a snarling man who looks him over, opens his mouth. Ignores his crying

Good. He will be for my son.

He is taken to a boy to be his playmate. The boy’s name is Renjiro Yamaoka. They become friends but there are rules. Renjiro must always win. If Renjiro hits him, he must accept it.

He goes with Renjiro to reading and fighting classes, but not as an equal—he must downplay his abilities. He is there to amuse. A living toy. And like a toy, he becomes dull. After a decade, he is cast off to work like the other servants. From then on, Renjiro looks at Hachi with bitterness, as if embarrassed of the bond he had with a commoner.

As Renjiro comes of age, he assumes the duties of a samurai. Beneath his façade of discipline and mercy is cruelty. He leaves scars on Hachi.

Renjiro boards a ship and Hachi goes with him. The Yamaoka family influence is set to extend to a new territory. Hachi pulls a cart of supplies aboard. A storm hits within hours of casting off. Tossed from bow to stern, Hachi grabs Renjiro’s hand as the samurai is nearly thrown overboard.

He wants to let go but he sees the face of the boy that was his only friend. He pulls him aboard.

A second to catch his breath.

A thunderous crash.

Parts of the hull explodes into splinters. He’s thrown to the deck. Through the ocean’s spray, he sees Renjiro, a jagged piece of wood pierced through his neck. Renjiro clutches his throat, tries to hold in the blood, his eyes wide as they fade into a furious, reluctant expression of death.

The ship comes apart.

Hachi awakens on a beach amidst debris and corpses. Nearby is a chest he brought aboard. He breaks it open, pulls out Renjiro’s armor, katana, and the Yamaoka family crest.

Hachi will never speak his true name again. On this day he becomes the samurai, Renjiro Yamaoka.
76312C34446A681B474B2483EC0CCA8D:
Renjiro… Hachi…

Who are you?

Too late to erase the lie now.

So, it is Renjiro who rides into the next town. A commoner bows her head as he passes. Nearby, a few men speak, glances cast in Renjiro’s direction. He pretends to ignore them. Muttered words reach his ears.

Father to an oni…

…evil blood. Not a real samurai…

Yamaoka butchers… come to kill…

Behind him, someone grabs his armor and attempts to pull him from his horse. He moves with the motion, spinning from his mount to land on his feet, a hand to his blade. The sudden fear struck in those around him stokes their anger. Shouted words become waves of indistinguishable sound. They demand answers to questions he cannot hear. A club slams against him. A hand yanks at his mask. Rai-Fu whinnies and runs.

Renjiro moves his hand to his sword.

No.

He cannot act as his son would. He would rather die than let the Yamaoka name drown in shame and blood.

A blow from behind pushes him to the ground. Strikes resonate through the armor to his ribs. He pushes his hand against his blade, ensures the frantic grips that pull at him cannot unsheathe it.

The strikes continue until the crowd’s anger is quenched. They walk away, spitting and laughing.

He pulls himself from the mud, whistling for Rai-Fu. Nothing. The horse lies at the roadside, his body still. Later, when Renjiro is beyond the sight of others, he will clutch his wounds and grieve.
2042CFEC473B2ADF8180BB9EA8342D89:
Renjiro examines his bruises. Nothing serious. But the violence… how did it come to this?

He remembers when Kazan was a young boy, shouting angrily.

They called me Imposter Noble! They sung and they laughed.

The guilt bears down on Renjiro. When he assumed the Yamaoka name, he could not convince everyone in the village of his lie. The lone survivor of a shipwreck, his only proof of identity being armor, a blade, and a family crest—it was a suspicious story. Were it not for what he learned as the playmate to a noble, he’d likely have been caught. But he was well-spoken, knew how to read, and could fight like a samurai. It dispelled most doubts.

Most.

The whisperings of an Imposter Noble would never be fully silenced. It fueled a rage in Kazan. Renjiro tried to teach his son patience and humility. He wonders what else he could have done.

I suppose I could have taught him the truth.
E57724344A43AE32CF7F15BDA55F66C7:
Renjiro sees Kazan ahead in the moon’s dim glow. His son is a hulking man, even more intimidating under slabs of armor.

They stop ten feet apart, two silhouettes in the night.

The unmasked face, barely illuminated by the moon, is his son’s—not an oni, but a boy, intoxicated on power he wields over the weak. It is Renjiro’s duty to punish the crime and return honor to the Yamaoka name.

Kazan is not just powerful but fast. He preys on weakness.

The men unsheathe their katanas. Renjiro assumes a defensive stance. He focuses on his injuries, the bruises over his body. His shoulder drops, sword dipping slightly. Kazan reacts, taking an aggressive stance. Renjiro exhales, pushes the pain away, hones in on his target. In a split-second he straightens up and lunges. His blade finds an opening in Kazan’s armor, drawing blood.

Kazan stumbles, his neck exposed. Eyes focused, blade ready, Renjiro shouts with grief, brings his sword back and—hesitates.

The kanabo crashes into Renjiro’s head, smashing the mask from his face.

Agony. The taste of blood in what feels like a gaping wound. He hears his son, far away, wailing. His heart races, gushing blood from his body and then… slows. Calmness descends. Ethereal dreams fade into nothing…

Silence.

A lack of anything.

A whisper?

A tug at his barely conscious mind.

The blood on his skin turns to ice. He shivers. Someone is there.

Kazan? Go play, boy. Let me sleep.

Kazan. His son… a child. Still young enough to be saved. He follows him through the fog as though his consciousness drifts through a storm.

There is something I must tell you, Kazan.

Renjiro lies in the dirt. The boy is gone. There is fire ahead, strange men and women huddled around it.

Kazan?

Something pulls his ankle. He kicks. His arm is wrenched back. He resists, lurching forward—he’s punished for it, his limb nearly torn from its socket. A spidery talon wraps across his bloody, broken face. Another grips his body, another his leg. It drags him through darkness, twisting, pulling, squeezing, as if unsure whether to abduct, strangle, or tear him apart.

He opens his mouth to scream. Black fog pours out.
36A12C8844F26B5E705B33BEFEBE9149:
Once upon a time, there were two brothers separated by black fog. There was Wilhelm Grimm, the adventurer, who strayed too far and never returned. And there was Jacob Grimm, the skeptic, who ventured into the darkness to find his wayward brother. 

Jacob rode for days and nights beyond measure, for time did not exist in this new land. In his travels he found other lost souls, victims of the monstrous fog. None of them could be saved. And everywhere he went, Jacob found visions of the stories he collected with his brother, brought to life before his very eyes. 

In his darkest moments, Jacob wondered if this was how his own story would end. Tired. Hungry. Lost in the infinite nothing, never to see Wilhelm again. 

It was just when he felt the last of his strength leave him that Jacob saw a flicker of hope. The warm glow of a fire deep in the distant trees. Desperation pushed him onward, blinding him to the terrors that lay on either side of him: shadows fighting between the trees, the bleached and shattered bones of great beasts, and more such things. 

On he ran, until the bright clearing was within reach. And what he saw there brought Jacob to tears.
15F87B3C44B015AFC384318CD76E2CED:
The tables in this clearing surrounded a great wooden goose and overflowed with the most succulent foods Jacob had ever seen. Fruits that glowed in the firelight, and sausages and roasted meats that glistened. Pitchers filled to the spout with hearty goat's milk. 

It was more than the starving man could have ever hoped for. He ate and drank greedily, without a care for who left this feast here or for whom it was meant. 

Jacob ate until he felt sick, and only then did he hear the chanting in the distance. His eyes searched the trees, and he saw dancing torchlight drawing closer and closer. These must be the guests on their way to the feast, he thought to himself. A voice in his mind told him that he was in a bloody trap. Whoever these guests were, they would not take kindly to an intruder such as him. 

Jacob scurried like a rat beneath one of the tables, away from the approaching parade of torch-wielding dinner guests. His curiosity kept him from running away, and from beneath the table, he waited to see what would happen next.
2FF9D7A04C4F8FE732541D8E39261A31:
Jacob watched as the parade of terror dragged his brother Wilhelm into the clearing and threw him into the wooden goose. Their leader, the demon who wore the rotting boar’s head, declared the beginning of the feast. 

Jacob knew there would be no other time to act. He crawled out from beneath the table, slinking around the clearing like a desperate animal. Acrid smoke from the burning torches filled the air above them, but the party guests did not notice or did not care. 

No one saw Jacob creep to the open entrance into the goose. Inside that wooden effigy, the two brothers embraced and wept. They readied themselves for their escape, but it was too late. They watched helplessly as the opening to the effigy was sealed shut, trapping them inside. 

“Light the offerings,” cried the Boar-Headed Leader to his guests. “We have caught them, and we will have them!”
6024C5344720FF675FA1419E66A7BDF3:
Portia stands at the bow of the ship. Stares at her notebook. A list of names, half crossed out. She has memorized every name, every alias, but she reads it each day nonetheless. 

She recently got a lead on one of the crew members. Andreas. He’s successfully covered his tracks for years, but he is getting sloppy. They all get sloppy eventually.  

A sharp bark rings out from below deck. She only bought Dagmar recently, but she has proven invaluable as a guard dog and rat hunter. Portia calls to her first mate, walks down the stairs. 

The poodle crouches defensively near a crate of hard tack. Portia unsheathes her blade as her first mate arrives. Cracks the crate open. Prepares to skewer any vermin she finds. 

What she finds, though, is a young woman, no older than 20, curled in a ball, dagger grasped tightly in her hand. The first mate drags her from the crate. 

Looks like we got a stowaway, cap’n. 

Portia puts her blade against the woman's chest, considers killing the woman, throwing the body overboard. To Portia’s surprise, the woman does not flinch. Her eyes harbor a steely fearlessness.  

What is your name? 

Her voice is hoarse, tired, but defiant. Nell.  

Portia is shorthanded after their last battle. For now, at least, she decides the girl is more valuable alive than dead. 

Nobody eats for free on my ship, Nell. You’ll work if you want to live.
A35DC525415453775F09F6BF0C68D30C:
The crew works long hours to make up for the lost sailors. They are exhausted. To Portia's surprise, though, none work harder than Nell. 

She approaches the new recruit. You.  

Nell keeps scrubbing, does not look up. Dagmar snarls again.  

Your ears broken? Portia kicks the brush from Nell's hand. She finally looks up. 

You're a hard worker. I like that. But you have to be prepared for our mission. 

Nell stares at Portia, unblinking. What mission is that? 

Killing every last member of the bastard Molak's crew. 

Nell's face flashes the briefest sign of anger. So it's a mission of revenge. 

Call it what you want. But I will not rest until it is done. 

Nell reaches for the brush, gets back to work. I can't remember the last time I rested.
83DF67994C75DF5F3E159797BBDEF9C4:
After weeks of tracking, Portia's crew tracked Andreas to a ramshackle cabin. Andreas was slumped over in his chair, drunk, as if he knew that death was coming. One brutal strike was all it took to cross his name off the list.  

With the modest riches he had collected now in their coffers, the crew celebrates with a barrel of rum in the crisp autumn air. Portia puts on a gregarious face, but the victory feels hollow. The blood-soaked path she walks has always been grim, but has never felt quite this empty. She looks at her book again... three dozen names, half of them crossed out... her entire purpose minimized to lines on paper. 

How long have you been doing this? 

Portia turns around. Nell's face is as dour as ever.  

Since you were a child, I'd wager. And there is still so much to do. 

Nell takes a seat across from her. Is it worth it? 

Portia is taken aback by the question. I do it because it must be done. Worth doesn't factor into it. 

In the moonlight, Nell's features are softened. Like a lost child. Unfamiliar, but familiar.  Right... no other option. 

You can either let the world walk all over you, or you can put your boot on the world's neck. 

Portia studies Nell's face. Senses a kind of understanding the others on her crew have ever shown. After a few minutes, Nell sits up, turns toward her quarters. 

I hope it's all worth it, cap'n.
6BB1DE3A48F5F31F896CB180F48C846A:
Portia's eyes shoot open as she hears Dagmar's urgent barks. The closet in her room bursts open and a figure leaps at her. The attacker's momentum immediately shifts as Dagmar smashes her into the wall, knocking the blade away. Dagmar’s eyes gleam red in the torchlight. She goes for the jugular. 

At the last possible moment, Portia hisses and the dog freezes. She rolls out of bed, places a heavy foot on the woman's chest.  

I wondered when you'd make your attempt. 

Portia presses her foot down, squeezing the wind out of Nell. What is it, then? Why have you decided to throw your life away tonight? 

Nell stares back, bloody, but still proud. Speaks barely above a whisper. 

For Ledley. 

Portia recognizes the name. She would never forget any of the names. Four years ago… one of the junior members of Molak’s crew. He was hard to find, not because he was clever, but because he was so… unremarkable. When she found him, he had returned to his hometown, where he was living a quiet life caring for… 

…his sister.
E41900BE43582CF6AEC67E88B1FDF723:
They drop anchor just off the coast of an untouched island. Portia walks Nell, bound and gagged, to the port side of the ship.  

The crew shouts and jeers. Run her through! Tar her! Feed her to the fish!  

The resolve has not left Nell's eyes. She stares forward defiantly as she is marched towards the edge of the deck.  

Portia gestures grandly to the crew. I don't suffer fools. I don't give up on the mission. And I don't let those who cross me survive. Portia shoves Nell so roughly that she almost falls overboard; Portia quickly grabs her shirt and jerks her back onto the deck.  

But we'll give her a fair chance, won't we? Only a mile from shore... maybe she'll be able to make it! All she has to do is learn to swim with her arms and legs tied. 

The crew laughs riotously. Portia whips Nell around, looks her square in the eyes. The captain drops the act, whispers so that only Nell can hear. 

My mission is not done. If you still hold hate in your heart for me when it's over, you'll find me again. 

Portia subtly slips Nell's blade under the ropes that bind her wrists. Gives the slightest of nods. And shoves her overboard into the inky-black sea.
41DB7FD94C291453A2018FB2009304C6:
Julian leans against Mikaela’s car, running his finger along the passenger door. He tugs at his arm warmer, looking up to see Mikaela leaving her house and heading his way, a slight hop in her step. She’s the one person who gets him, scars and all. She holds up a set of car keys. 

Got ‘em! 

Julian never had a doubt. Mikaela’s mom isn’t the type to put up barriers around her daughter. She wants her to be happy—especially after her father’s death—even if it means sending her off to explore an abandoned roadside hotel that’s said to be haunted. Julian pitched the idea for the road trip last week. It’s been too long since they swapped the horrors of high school for a different kind. They can check out the old murder site and Mikaela can find inspiration for her stories while he shoots footage for his rural decay documentary. Somewhere in there, maybe he could vent his frustrations a bit. Between school, family, and assholes, his veins feel like they’re going to burst. 

They get into the car and Julian grabs the CD case off the dash. It’s filled with generic silver discs, titles written on them with black marker. Most are filled with songs that Julian and Mikaela chose together. He glances over at Mikaela, waiting for her to start the car. Her fingers are pattering along the steering wheel. 

Hold on, I invited—ah, there she is. 

The back door opens and a figure clad in black with a hint of pink shuffles in. Sable. 

His bangs drift down his forehead, obscuring his rolling eyes. He doesn’t like surprises. His voice is tinged with disappointment when he speaks. 

Hey, Sable. 

She says hi in her dead-girl tone, so low on emotion that he barely catches the hidden meaning in it:  

I didn’t expect you here either.
214C026C4D30EC9B5E3298878AD4BA4D:
Julian peers through the passenger window. The pissed off lyrics from a pop-punk song are going through his head. He counts burnt-out streetlights leading to a dead neon sign, the hotel alone on the highway’s edge. The trio exits the car, the scene reminding Julian of a dozen horror movies he can’t quite place. 

In the lobby is a dust-filled gloom of antique carpet and upholstered chairs. Mikaela runs over to the desk’s service bell, taps it and smiles as a ding echoes through the lifeless room. Julian pulls out his video camera and gestures for the others to follow as he looks down a hall. Sable calls for him to wait. 

From a backpack, she grabs a box of salt and spills it into a circle. 

We do a séance first. You don’t barge in without saying hi to the spirits. 

Mikaela takes a seat beside Sable. Julian begrudgingly follows suit. 

Sable pulls out an audio recorder, then goes through a process involving incense, effigies, and an offering bowl. She opens a string-wrapped cloth to reveal a small knife. 

Julian recoils at the sight of the blade, tugging nervously at his arm warmer. 

Seriously? We’re going from spirit boards to bloodletting? 

Sables pushes the tip of the blade to her thumb. 

Calm it down, we only need a drop each. 

Julian grabs at Sable’s wrist. 

I’m not doing that. Put it away!
267C77A4433A59559DFA449BDFAA3490:
Julian clutches at his bloody palm, a jagged cut carved through the skin. 

Sable freezes. 

It’s ceremonial. It’s not sharp. 

It’s sharp enough! 

Mikaela frantically tries to defuse the situation, but Julian’s focus is on the pain-fueled anger that centers solely on Sable. Where did she even come from? It started as Julian and Mikaela, then somehow, as if from nowhere, Sable appeared and inserted herself. Now the goth girl’s always in the spotlight. 

In his anger he says this. Or some of it. It’s cluttered, uncertain, but raw.  

Sable faces down his glower. 

It’s been me and Mikaela since we were kids. You were never a part of this. You inserted yourself into our story. 

Julian searches for words but finds only the urge to yell. He looks to the dark hallway and chooses it over the discomfort of the now, leaving Mikaela and Sable behind.
389F59604350B0C906803F9331FDC551:
Sable quietly packs up her seance gear. Mikaela offers her a smile. 

Julian just needs a minute. I wanted to bring you two together but maybe I shouldn’t have sprung it on you. I just want everyone to get along. 

A sudden scream carries through the hall. Julian. Then, a crash. 

Mikaela breaks into a sturdy sprint. 

Sable follows through darkened halls, barely able to see the walls that guide her. Somewhere she’s turned around and finds herself alone. She nearly trips over Julian, his ankle wedged between broken floorboards. He gestures to a nearby door. 

In there, I saw… I don’t know, something came at me. 

Sable steels her nerves and walks to the darkened room.
23A70ED64630DB4936E809BD274D778D:
It’s not the chilling, ethereal grip of a specter that reaches around Sable’s hand but… polyester. The figure Julian saw was nothing but a bedsheet blowing in the breeze.  

She returns to Julian who has freed his ankle from the floorboards. Having calmed down, he looks embarrassed. Sable offers him a hand and, after a moment’s hesitation, he takes it. As he reaches up, scars stretch from the edge of his arm warmer. The thin lines are only there for a moment before they disappear beneath the fabric. Sable recalls his panic when she pulled the knife from her backpack. She glances away from his arm, pretending not to notice, looking instead to the dark room she had just explored.  

I didn’t see anything in there. 

Julian nods, as if expecting mockery. She continues. 

But I believe you. Wicked things are out there. They torment people, sometimes silently, in a way others don’t notice. 

On their way to the lobby, they reunite with Mikaela. She runs up and gives them both a hug. Sable retrieves the audio recorder from her backpack and looks to Julian. 

Sightings are rare, maybe you could be my first interview? 

The red-light glows on the recorder and, after a moment’s hesitation, Julian begins to recount the scene of a shadowy apparition. Temporary as it may be, for a moment in time the two are in sync, their divergent tales coming together, misfit teens with a taste for the unusual, operating on a single wavelength.
54C497A549DA185E9A17C18B4EC71AD0:
There is a reprieve this night in the asylum, and Sally does what any sane person would do—she clings to it with all her strength. The weight that sits in her chest melts away, allowing for one starving breath. The scent of sweat and dusty linen is willed from her mind, replaced with memories of tomatoes and fresh soil. Her feet take her down the hall, heels clicking, echoing into an expanse of shadows. She does not allow herself to see the stains on the walls or the fracture in the window's pane. She could draw them from memory but, for this moment, they cease to exist.

As Sally reaches the end of the hall, she peers into a patient's room, illuminated by a blade of moonlight cutting across the floor. A young girl, sitting atop the bed, flinches at the oncoming shadow. Only as Sally walks into the moonlight does the girl release her grip on a bundle of sheets. Sally offers a sympathetic smile to her… the Anxious Girl. The asylum's file lists her name as Marion but the staff have codes for each patient. The Catatonic Boy, the Sweaty Codger, the Anxious Girl. Everything they are summarized into two words.

Sally sits on the edge of the bed, braiding the Anxious Girl's dry, brittle hair. Did you visit the community room today? The Anxious Girl hugs her pillow. I stayed here. A light moan carries through the hall, the first indication that peace will soon be broken. Sally does her best to ignore it, weaving one strand of hair over another. Did you know that room has a chair by the window? You can see the robins building a nest in the trees. The Anxious Girl looks to the hallway, her shoulders tensing as she listens to the distant moan. Sally gently rubs the girl's shoulder, wordlessly offering her sympathy. They sit for a short time until a scream carries through the hallway.
33F098404FEF3C5A722A43B4760B329D:
Sally marches down the hall to the source of the scream. Patients, each in their own rooms, react, an interlude of cries and shrieks joining in, accompanied by the thumping of a head slamming into a wall. The volume builds, louder and more chaotic, until finally, as if reaching a crescendo, a patient howls. Sally rushes into a room, moving towards a hideously scarred woman, restrained to the bed, whose scream slowly dies into soft, mirthful laughter. Did you enjoy the song, sweet nurse? I call it Concerto of Lunatics.

The asylum is wide awake now, alive, anxious, the scattered shrieks and moans of patients ricocheting through the halls. Sally's chest tightens, as she struggles to breathe. Why… why must you rile them? The Broken Woman smiles beneath the swath of bandages over her scarred face. Through two small holes, mismatched eyes—blue and orange—sparkle. Oh, sweet nurse, what are the jesters for if not a laugh? Sally knows to step away, knows there is nothing to gain from arguing, yet she cannot restrain herself. They are humans and, sick as they may be, they deserve sympathy. This is a line Sally has told herself many times over the years, though that is all it has become—a line; a series of carefully rehearsed words pushed through chapped lips. Perhaps this is why the Broken Woman chuckles as if trading quips with a friend. They deserve sympathy? Most have contributed nothing but pain, and the others have contributed nothing at all.
E039B381492DF41F7B0AD89CFA58907C:
Sally makes no attempt to suppress her disgust as she looks at the Broken Woman's smile. You would criticize your fellow patients for bringing nothing to this world, yet what have you provided? The Broken Woman awkwardly sits up on her bed, pulling at her restraints like a restless marionette. I have provided more to this world than a thousand missionaries. When I saw sickness, I did not coddle it, feed it, wipe the tears from its eyes—I cleansed it! The Broken Woman sees she has Sally's attention. If we want humanity to survive, we must be its custodians, sweet nurse. And yet… we have allowed an infection to fester—the evidence pervading these walls. The Broken Woman pauses, allowing her point to settle. Shrieks and moans from the mentally insane echo through the halls.

Sally feels her nerves tighten with each chaotic noise that comes her way. She has little desire to argue, yet duty compels. Are you not within these walls too? Would that not make you part of the infection? The Broken Woman smiles as if expecting this question. I am the solution, condemned to the halls of the infected. Like you, I was a nurse. But I served not the patients but the greater good. With one simple injection I removed the weak from the gene pool. I watched them in their death throes, knowing my actions were backed by honest science so few have the strength to trust. And do you know what the courts called me for following logic? Insane!
054046FA4B79F55B8C85D1A370510A96:
The days pass, but Sally's unsure how many. She always finds herself back in the asylum, tending to the frantic, the violent, the feeble. Down the hall, the Bad Man has slipped his restraints again. Like a wolf, he shows no motive but to prowl for the weak, and it appears he's found his prey. He drags the naked body of the Rancid Son by the ankles. Blood spills from the Son's head. Sally does not know if the man is dead. Calling for help, she sprints down the hall with a syringe filled of sedatives. There are no other nurses to come to her aid. Financial restrictions have seen to that. She considers that she is running to her death this time, but there is something involuntary in her movements, as if she has become a spectator. The Bad Man lets go of the Rancid Son's ankles and turns his attention to Sally. He fails to notice Harvey Kavanagh, the plump orderly, round the corner behind him. Harvey slams The Bad Man into the floor as he's done to so many patients. Sally jabs a sedative into the Bad Man's neck. The Bad Man sags in place and with a look of bewilderment falls to the ground.

The decrepit hall is silent. Sally looks over the scene at her feet. Kavanagh's sizable frame hefts up and down as he catches his breath, thick arm slung over The Bad Man who rests peacefully. The Rancid Son, either unconscious or dead, lies beneath them with Kavanagh's boot pressed against his nostril. The smear of blood from his head goes on for thirty feet down the hall before curling into an adjacent room. Sally laughs to stop herself from screaming.
9551C2824A7C7B362B7EDDA2A4142AD1:
Sally finds herself in the Broken Woman's room. The mismatched eyes of the Broken Woman appear sympathetic as the sunlight shimmers over them, yet she speaks with sharpened words. Shame about that bloody disturbance yesterday. Boys like that are made a certain way… not built for civil society. The big, brutish one, well, it is as plain as the skin on his face. And the other, oh, the other one hides it well. But have you looked at his family name? That will explain everything.

Sally wills herself to think of a gentle lake, lilies and—no… all she can see are the grimy asylum walls and bloody bandages. There are no gentle breezes to distract her, only the Broken Woman's voice prodding deeper. Did you not have a husband, sweet nurse? I recall the newspaper article… hand to heart, my dear, I cried at his unfortunate death. You would have had beautiful babies. To now be here, a widow of pure genes, serving the filth of the world—such a turn of events.

Sally gets up, leaving a bandage half-wrapped. Her feet shuffle imprecisely as she moves for the door. She tries to push her thoughts away, knows she shouldn't think it, but—it is such cruelty. Her love was pure, her husband pure, and those who live in these halls are anything but. Yet these sick, twisted beasts, receive the care and attention deserved to the man she lost.

Her throat catches on each breath. Her vision blurs. She wants to run but knows it's no use. No matter where she goes, she always finds herself back in these halls. With swirling thoughts, one stark realization breaks through: it is not she who keeps the insane confined to these halls, but the insane who confine her.

She falls to the unforgiving floor.
42E2E7404A6575E8CB5A1F9F5A84E183:
A lush green field dotted with salmon-colored lilies and patches of pine trees surround the lake. The colors are more vibrant than Sally remembers, and though it smells of fresh rain, the sky is clear. Andrew sits next to her on a blanket, his blonde hair nearly white in the sun. She wears the dress he had bought her. A symbol of my love, he had written on the card, and for a man of few words it meant many.

He wipes the grass stains from his calloused hands and turns to Sally. We should get home. The lake will still be here tomorrow. A cold breeze sweeps through the meadow, bringing with it the scent of sweat and dusty linen. She grips his wrist with both hands. Just one more minute, please. One more.

She hears saws ripping through lumber, the sound heightening with each violent slash. Tighter, she holds Andrew's wrist, pressing her head into his shoulder and bracing herself. An immense tree slams to the ground behind her, sending twigs and dirt into the air. One after another, they come down in booming, ground-shaking jolts. Sally coughs through a cloud of dust, keeping her grip on Andrew the entire time.

A bead of blood trickles down his arm, coming to rest on her finger. She looks up to see her husband's skull broken open, spilling blood and chunks of brain. One stark white eye looks out from the carnage, focused intently on her. We would have had beautiful babies, Sally.

She collapses into the crimson muck of his chest and cries. The skin on her hands flakes away, turning to dust. She loses her grip on him. Everything she was, down to the dress she wore, decays, blown away in the wind.

The sweaty hands of Kavanagh shake her as she awakes on the asylum floor.
654C2E5B43938852B4F04E984CFA0F01:
She's in the hallway again. The scent, the stains, her heels clicking—it's the same. Occasional moans and shouts carry from nearby rooms, short bursts of mania or terror that emerge and intermingle: The Concerto of Lunatics.

Sally enters the Anxious Girl's room and sits at the foot of her bed. The girl flinches but, after a second's pause, lifts herself up. Illuminated under moonlight, she offers a timid yet warm smile. Sally takes three strands of the girl's hair and begins to weave a braid. Did you see the robins today? But Sally doesn't wait for the girl's answer. Another day hiding, wasn't it? And what about the robins? They will be dead by the time you leave this room.

The girl's shoulders tense and Sally feels herself do the same. She takes a deep breath, attempting to calm herself. As she parts the hair back from the Anxious Girl's skull, she spies tiny, writhing creatures. An infestation of lice crawls through the girl's hair. Sally pulls her hand back and slaps the girl across her face. Filthy!

Their eyes lock, confusion and startlement among them both. Tears trickle down the Anxious Girl's helpless face, wet chin trembling. Sally takes a step back. She thinks to apologize, to explain the stress she's been under, but something in her refuses. Filthy girl! She storms from the room.
CDBA0729463DA973AE45B9AA44A86D12:
Sally, her face emotionally void, sits next to the Broken Woman's bed. She finds herself more and more in this position, listening to the woman ramble. The Broken Woman fidgets with her restraints, fixated on an unscarred piece of skin at the base of her hand. Purification comes in many forms. We must all make sacrifices. She curls a finger inwards and scratches at the clean piece of skin until it's torn off. For the most grotesque offenders—the genetic abominations—we must take extreme measures. Otherwise, you get… well, the results surround you.

Sally sits motionless, her tired eyes the only indication that she's conscious. The Broken Woman speaks as if chatting with a friend over tea. Do you know what I could do? I could tell you the ingredients for my special injection… the one I used on my patients. A quick little prick and they'll writhe as if a purifying fire burns within. A fitting way to deal with inhuman filth, wouldn't you say? Are you hearing me, sweet nurse? You don't have to be their servant anymore.
9BB187174FC8FCB5C9E9CBA8D445B351:
Sally feels the asylum closing in on her. Whispers of paranoid lunatics spill through the cracks. She wonders how long she can walk this hallway, questions if it ever ends. She passes the Catatonic Boy in his wheelchair, staring deep into the walls. He gazes in her direction though his eyes look through her. Has the trial begun? He lets out a scream, pausing as if having startled himself, then laughs.

Harvey Kavanagh, the Fat Orderly, emerges from a patient's room and gives her a smile. The skin on his neck dangles as he moves, glistening with sweat. A thick coat of hair covers his arms and curls over the collar of his shirt. His eyes move from Sally's feet upwards, pausing on her chest until he realizes she's watching him. His eyes dart to examine the floor as he nervously licks his mouth.

Ahead, the Foul Girl skips gracefully, enjoying her first day out of restraints in a month. She hums a pleasant tune, tracing her hand over the wall. As Sally approaches, the Girl tilts her head forward. She lets out a long, guttural sound, heaving her diaphragm until vomit splashes onto the floor. Content with herself, she smiles and skips on.

Sally continues, giving no thought to cleaning the mess. She sees the Shoeless Imbecile sitting by the broom closet. Thick strands of blood drip from his mouth. With precise rhythm he slams his jaw into the doorframe six times, digs at his gums, and pulls out a tooth. He peers at Sally as if she's the strangest thing he's ever seen.

Sally looks out at the hallway, stretching on forever. She stops, accepting what she's tried to suppress: the sickness can grow no more.
D4D6C3994A9787C9D27905A0C8D766B6:
Sally fills the syringe as the Broken Woman instructed. Thick, dark liquid swirls within, a night sky void of stars. The helpless anxiety that crippled her vanishes under a sea of calm.

Though her heels click with each step, she feels as if she floats; as if everything she's to do has been determined, requiring only the gentlest breeze to push her forward. She sees the sickness clearly. It has infected all. But the most hideous, is the one who refuses to face it; the dog that doesn't know it's a dog. And so, she makes her way to the Broken Woman's room.

Strange how, for all the woman's wisdom, she is blind to her impurities. Though she removes the blemishes from her skin, she fails to judge the mismatched eyes that gaze at her in the mirror. But no amount of carving can remove genetics. Such a case requires extreme measures.

Sally grips the syringe and prepares for what's to come. There is such filth that permeates the asylum—if she is to cleanse it all, she had best begin.
A41A35CD47B33FDF4EFCAE9DF1B60175: I am going through some past scribblings and the notes of the previous unknown occupants, and I realize I should at least try to organize them. Reading these notes, I decipher several voices who I am aptly calling the unknown few who like myself had a fixation with the Entity and who like myself had an ability to experience the memories encoded in the fog. I will include my past scribblings and number them as best as I can, referring to them as notes obscura, or just obscura, to try and piece together how long I've actually been here. I think I may have found my first ramblings amongst the half-destroyed journals of the unknown occupants who struggled with infinite possibilities of whiling away the time except the one they probably missed the most. The one I miss the most—friendship, companionship, sitting with my father drinking whiskey and watching the Ancients swim across the night sky, or just losing time with a friend in a hearty conversation about the merits of art, music, laughter and stories. All I have now are the memories of others. Second-hand experiences that constantly remind me of things lost and half-remembered.
1D7BD0E44CAE2A4A70133EBBEA4CEB8F: I've found scattered about this tower countless journals from previous occupants. Occupants might not be the best way to describe them. Prisoners would be more fitting. Eight or nine of them from the distinct voices I deciphered in the manifold journals I read with surprising interest and alacrity. Some of these unknown prisoners shared my unusual penchant for beer, whiskey and stories of the macabre. Others seemed to be raving lunatics writing not journals but senseless notes—notes from the absurd I call them—strange musings and endless contradictions about places and characters observed and consciously or unconsciously improperly described. These notes from the absurd seem to start with unintelligible gibberish are quite different from anything I've seen or read, as though written by someone driven by madness or some other motive to undermine any attempt to make sense of this world. Along with the notes I found illustrations and survivor statements from police files and thousands of short stories in a dark chamber in the basement.  They had been piled up and set ablaze but quickly extinguished with some sort of a putrid, rotting sludge. I cleaned the chamber and stacked all the stories in piles to go through and organize at a later date. For the time being I see no reason to remove them from what I am now calling the Chamber of Blood.
A0D21C0B467BAA2C2C13F29B1E531AB9: I was listening to a podcast of creepy stories with my friends… Adrien… Mia… Tina… and Bill. I can't remember which one of us figured how to do it… but we realized that the stories were codes to pass on coordinates of locations of interest for some group or cult or whatever. There was nothing but overgrown ruins. But I remember this unnatural black fog and it was like we were at the asylum but some other version of it. It was really strange. And that's when we saw this thing… this giant samurai with a demon mask lurking about as though it had stepped out of one world and into another. He killed Mia first. I don't remember what happened exactly… I just saw… I saw her head thump and tumble across the ground. Not long after a man who called himself Hans and who identified himself as a detective arrived and asked me questions about what I had seen. He took some notes and seemed a bit strange. Then when he heard the sirens approaching, he disappeared just like that. When the police arrived, the fog was gone leaving only the… the… hacked remains of my friends. 97E21C444E5A07CB1D55EA82020109E2: Ha! Bubble gum tuna on Tuesday! Sir regal Dwight in a thicklish purple robe and golden crownee steps out into the courtyard and greets all the peasants with good words and pizza. The kingdom cheers and roars.
B5E1DCD641933E738963EE97F547CE2C: NOTES FROM THE ABSURD. EMPEROR DWIGHT.
B3FF77D64C5D30B895D5C5B2AF1AC450:
Chamber of Blood. Harbinger of Hell. Evil Eyes. 1.

Haddie Kaur lifted her chai tea, let the steaming, spicy cardamom and cinnamon elixir sooth down her throat, and set down her stainless-steel cup in the small dhaba near her ancestral village of Mohi. The tea warmed her insides, yet she shivered cold with a nameless terror that mocked and poked at her like a formless apparition, reminding her that all wasn't what it seemed and that there were nameless things that went bump in the night. Ever since Haddie could remember she had seen and heard things beyond the veil, and she even had vague recollections of the day her parents disappeared while they were vacationing when she was five years old. She remembered the whispers, the approaching darkness, and the sense that somehow they were in another reality. She didn't remember much about that time, but she remembered being taken in by her French-Canadian godparents, the Rois, who raised her with their son, Jordan. Now Haddie and her older stepbrother Jordan were in India, filming episodes for their fairly successful web series 'Harbinger of Hell' with their uncle Stefan. A fan had sought them out after having watched one of their episodes about interdimensional overlaps which Haddie could sense, feel and even explore if her focus was right and she was able to 'tune in' as she so often described her process. As their luck would have it this mysterious benefactor had funded an entire expedition all over the world, giving her brother and uncle access to countless remote and classified areas of known paranormal activity and unexplainable disappearances. Haddie sipped her tea, listening to the villagers speak a language that reminded her of her disappeared father, and she suddenly heard a familiar voice and Quebecois accent that stood out from the rest calling out her name. A moment later Stefan entered the dhaba with Jordan. “I found the site of the massacre,” Stefan said. “Finish your tea, and let's get outta here!” Haddie sprang to her feet and followed her uncle and brother into the scorching hot day.
00F87AEE46089462703B6EAE65E3EF45:
Chamber of Blood. Harbinger of Hell. Evil Eyes. 2.

“The thugs were ambushed in the valley near the ruins of the old signaling fort,” a turbaned man with a beard said. “I'm not sure what you hope to find here. Most stay away from this place like the plague.” He stared at the older teens as if they were mad. “You should have returned to the hotel like your uncle. Nothing here but the eyes, and they're probably watching us right now.” Haddie and Jordan didn't answer or want to explain that their uncle didn't have the stomach for adventure, that he was more of a producer and that he was trying to finish off a horror novel he'd been working on for the last ten years. Ignoring the guide's nervous ramblings, Haddie studied the white stone bricks of the ruined fort and the surrounding caves with a strange feeling that they were being watched. The guide said, “The official story is a unit of British soldiers died fighting a band of thugees.” “And the unofficial story?” Haddie turned to him. The guide stared at her for a long moment. “The unofficial story is they turned their rifles and swords against each other. Something in these caves drove them mad.” Haddie absorbed this and closed her eyes while Jordan filmed the ruins and the caves. Calming her heart and silencing her mind, she began to hear the rising screams and cries of people being butchered. When she opened her eyes again, she could see the scintillating orange residual memories of British soldiers cutting down thuggee rebels. One thug seemed to be holding something important in his hands as he escaped the massacre. She walked through residual memories and approached the thug, starring at a piece of broken pillar in his hand. The thug desperately clambered over the rocks and rubble, charging into a nearby cave with the soldiers in hot pursuit. Jordan stepped up behind her. “Did you see anything?” Haddie nodded and pointed at the cave the thug had run into. The guide raised his eyebrows. “And that's my cue to go,” he said, turning his back on the siblings. “Not that I think you're both crazy… which I do… but I need to get home before my wife realizes I'm gone. It's my day to make rotis and pick up the kids from school.” Haddie and Jordan watched the guide disappear down the rocky, sun-baked valley. Then they turned and approached the gaping mouth of the cave. For a long moment they stared into the darkness without saying a word. Jordan turned on the flashlight of his cellphone and just as they prepared to enter, they heard the crunch of stone behind them. Brother and sister turned slowly to face the barrel of a rifle.
4280CD0A492A7C942AECED999B8D894C:
Chamber of Blood. Harbinger of Hell. Evil Eyes. 3.

Three men speaking an ancient, unknown language forced Haddie and Jordan through the dark and seemingly endless cave with flickering flashlights to illuminate the way. Somehow these captors knew Haddie had a gift and were barking orders for her in broken English to lead them to the place where the thuggee rebel had hidden the relic. She didn't recognize her captors but it wasn't the first time someone had forced her to find something with her special abilities. Haddie followed a trail of residual memories—memories and whispers only she could see and hear. She could sense they were walking through an 'overlap' of realities which heightened and reinforced her abilities in an inexplicable way. She followed the scintillating orange trail and froze when the residual soldiers suddenly disappeared. Then she started when the soldiers blinked back into existence and she heard desperate screams as something she couldn't make out attacked them. “What is it?” one of her captors asked. “She's seeing something,” Jordan said. “Let her do her thing.” “This better not be a trick!” Haddie watched the indiscernible creature rip the soldiers into an unrecognizable mess of flesh and gore. The creature then snatched the thug and dragged him screaming through a series of interconnecting tunnels. She chased after the fading memory, entering a small cavern as she watched the thug release the relic as the creature dragged him into a smaller tunnel that she imagined led to a feeding den. Memories burned out like dying embers to reveal a cavern of human bones piled over thick rotting sludge. Interestingly enough, I found seventeen versions of a story featuring a killer named Evan written by seventeen versions of the same author from the omniverse. Seventeen similar stories with sometimes subtle, sometimes significant differences. What I find particularly interesting is how the stories are written as fiction in one world and non-fiction in another. It reminds me of Universus Alveo… a theory that suggests that the human mind might very well be equipped with a powerful networking mechanism that reaches out to other worlds for wisdom and knowledge from our other-selves. Some can use their minds in this way and others can't. The theory suggests that those who have experienced trauma in their formative years detach from their reality, allowing them to explore other realities and worlds with relative ease. Artists like magicians and shamans see small things in the big, unexplainable endless dream that is the omniverse and they bring these ideas or insights back to entertain, enlighten and inspire the world. Fiction in one world, non-fiction in another. Everything is real, or nothing is. And here in the Chamber of Blood there are countless horror stories of every variety.  So many that it seems to me that one of the unknown prisoners was collecting these stories as a way to discover more about their imprisonment, the Entity and the terrible screams coming from the surrounding abyss. Whether this true or not, I'm not sure, but what I do know is I spent the whole night reading my favorite stories out loud like my father used to do by the fireplace. And the entire time I couldn't help but wonder… How?  How could anyone have accessed and assembled such a rich collection of notes, journals and stories? I have no immediate answer, but I suspect by the texture and density of the fog that I may be in a place as complex, mysterious and misunderstood as a black hole—a living, breathing, all-consuming black hole, the serpent of infinity that gorges on its tail, that eats itself endlessly as it spirals downward into the cosmic, Fibonacci stew that is life incomprehensible.
